setting: park (Hefei Feicui Lake scenic spot - lakeside urban scenic park with musical fountain and violin island)
design: mixed (soundwalk with 10 sampling points + on-site Likert questionnaire + SPL measurement + evening musical-fountain on/off comparison)
sample_n: 262 valid questionnaires of 273 collected (300 distributed), March 2023; plus 120 evening interviewees (60 with musical fountain on, 60 with fountain off)
exposure: Musical theme landscape fused with the site soundscape (musical fountain switched on vs off, violin island, broadcast music, fountain and bird sounds, traffic and construction noise); LAeq measured at 10 points ranged 42.1-74.5 dB(A)
behaviour_measure: Staying, resting and communicating at the musical fountain (proportion preferring to stay/rest/communicate; stayed vs passed by); visit purpose (entertainment and rest vs passing through), length of stay and number of visits used as behavioural predictors of soundscape satisfaction and comfort
measurement_method: self-report (soundwalk-based Likert questionnaire and on-site verbal interview at the fountain) + sensor (BSWA801 and Norsonic Nor121 sound level meters, 01dB software)
key_finding: With the musical fountain operating, perceived comfort and the share of visitors staying, resting or communicating were significantly higher than when it was off; visitors whose activity was entertainment or rest, who stayed longer, or who had visited more than five times reported higher satisfaction, and satisfaction/comfort peaked parabolically at 50-60 dB(A)
effect_stats: Comfortable or very comfortable 68.33% (fountain on) vs 43.33% (fountain off), p < .05; willing to stay, rest or communicate 68.33% vs 56.67%; entertainment/rest users vs passers-by, longer vs shorter stay, and >5 vs <5 visits all p < .05; sound sensitivity decreased with visit number p < .05; education p < .01; gender and age p > .05; LAeq 42.1-74.5 dB(A) with optimum 50-60 dB(A); n = 262, Cronbach alpha 0.741, KMO 0.757

country: Vietnam (field observation in Ho Chi Minh City); anechoic-chamber measurements in Japan
setting: street (Hoang Van Thu Street, congested urban arterial) with controlled anechoic-chamber acoustic measurement
design: mixed (weekday rush-hour roadside HD video and sound level meter observation + structured interviews + controlled anechoic-chamber horn experiment)
sample_n: 30 interviewees (10 experienced motorcycle taxi drivers, 20 university students commuting daily by motorcycle); weekday morning and evening rush-hour traffic recordings
exposure: Motorcycle horn-use behaviour classified as attention signals P1-P3 (single, double, triple presses of 0.5-0.7 s with 0.3-0.5 s intervals) and warning signals P4-P6 (single press > 1 s; short presses ending in a prolonged press), reproduced on a 125 cc electromechanical diaphragm horn and an electric horn
behaviour_measure: Horn-use pattern typology coded from rush-hour video and SLM recording plus interviews (number of presses, press duration, inter-press interval), and the resulting A-weighted LAeq,T over a fixed 1.5 s window, 1/3-octave spectra and directivity per pattern
measurement_method: observation (HD video plus calibrated sound level meter RION NL-28) + self-report (structured interviews)
key_finding: In congested Ho Chi Minh City traffic riders habitually use multi-press and prolonged horn patterns rather than the single press assumed by regulation, so the signalling behaviour itself raises emitted level by 13-17 dB(A) and shifts low- and high-frequency content, pushing street noise beyond WHO daytime guidance; the authors frame horn noise as a behavioural as well as a technical problem
effect_stats: P1 single press 87 dB(A); attention patterns about 103 dB and warning patterns above 104 dB; P2 - P1 approx. 14 dB(A); P4 - P1 13 dB(A); P5 - P4 3 dB(A); P6 - P1 17 dB(A); band-level differences up to 20 dB in ranges A1-A2; electric horn P1 94.8 dB, i.e. 17 dB above the diaphragm horn; field horns up to 112 dB; fundamental 387 Hz with energy peak near 3 kHz; horn emission broadly omnidirectional; no inferential statistics reported (NR)

country: UK (UCL-run online focus groups; participants based in Turkiye, Germany, UK, Italy, Ireland and Switzerland)
setting: street (urban streets as recalled and discussed by expert participants; data collected online)
design: survey (two online expert focus groups via Microsoft Teams; deductive thematic analysis with inductive refinement, NVivo 15, two-coder consensus)
sample_n: 12 experts (Turkish cohort n = 6, international cohort n = 6); separate pilot focus group n = 12 excluded from analysis
exposure: Street soundscape as experienced and discussed by experts: traffic and mechanical noise, ambulance and police sirens, natural sounds and water features, silence, religious and cultural soundmarks (adhan, church bells), station jingles, together with street geometry, greenery, lighting and temporal variation
behaviour_measure: Thematically coded behaviour reported in transcripts: route choice and detours, walking speed, orientation of pedestrian flows toward or away from sound sources, pausing to talk, gathering or leaving an area, accessibility-related movement, and coping/adaptive strategies such as bone-conduction headphones (Theme 4 referenced by 10 of 12 participants)
measurement_method: self-report (focus group transcripts transcribed and coded line-by-line in NVivo 15 by two researchers)
key_finding: Experts reported that street soundscapes steer pedestrian behaviour: soundmarks such as the adhan orient pedestrian flows and structure daily rhythms, aversive sounds prompt detours or withdrawal from an area, sound and lighting shape whether people pause to talk or gather, and adaptive strategies such as bone-conduction headphones are adopted; silence was a dilemma, read as safe or unsafe depending on pedestrian density
effect_stats: NR (qualitative; n = 12; 4 main themes, 16 subthemes, 34 codes, 102 coded instances; behaviour and perception themes each referenced by 10 of 12 participants; 7 of 10 Healthy Streets metrics directly referenced)
